title: Rashi on Avodah Zarah
text: Before the festivals of the idolaters 3 days it is forbidden to do business with them - and all of this is because he will go and thank his idol on the day of his festival: "borrowing" (sheilah) [refers to] things that need to be returned, like animals and vessels, as it is written (shemos 22:13) "when a man borrows from his neighbor..." "borrowing" (malveh) [refers to] things that don't need to be returned, like money, as it is written (ibid) "if you lend [someone from] my nation money" because malveh is when [money] is given to spend and he (the borrower) pays him (the lender) with other money
he's happy for another time - for tomorrow
Kelaneya: Free, such that it not give taxes ever. It was since it had rabbis in it, and Antoninus himself served before Rebbe, as per the below. And because of that, he was a friend of the rabbis.
Rabbi brought a man, placed him, etc.: That is to say, place your son over them and over you, and Tiberias will be be given into his hands.
And tell him, to your son, that he should let the dove fly from his hands. That is to say, that he should make Tiberias a free city, to release it from his yoke.
But let him say [it] to him publicly.
Perhaps they will cause him anguish, to Rabbi.
Performed a prohibited action: She had illicit intercourse.

He sent him, Antoninus to Rabbi, an herb, the name of which was gargira; orugue in [Old French]. And Rabbi understood: What do I have to do with this herb? It is certainly a sign (message) that he sent me. Gargira is that the heart of Gira was dragged (negrara) and drawn in with the adulterers. He knew how to study [the message from] Antoninus.
He sent him: Rabbi [sent] coriander (kusbarta); aillendre in [Old French]. That is to say, slaughter the daughter - kos barta (which means, kill daughter) - it is two words.
He sent him again: Antoninus [sent] leeks (karti); porels in [Old French]. That is to say, if so, my offspring will be cut off (yikaret).
He sent him again, lettuce (chasa): Laitugue in [Old French]. That is to say, have pity (chus) on her.
Matrata: Leather saddlebags, like big sacks.
With wheat in the opening of the sacks: As if they open the sacks, they will see wheat and they will not understand [its actual contents].
And those who come from them will bring forth to them: Those that come from among you will pay expenses (taxes) to the kings of Rome that will arise after me, relying upon that money.
Nekarta: A cave. It is [related to] the expression, nikrat hatzur (the cleft of the rock, Exodus 33:22).
To Rabbi's house: To study Torah.
Would minister to him: He would serve before him at the meal.
There is Edom: The verse is situated in Geihinnom.
Accustomed (Hergel) matter: Intercourse. Hergel is a beginning, as in (Avot 3:13), "accustom (margilin) [a person] to promiscuity" - they lead to [and that is a beginning].
She passed wind (gas).

And some say, because of the story of Beruriah: As one time, she mocked that which the Sages said (Kiddushin 80b), "The conviction of women is weak about them." And he said [to himself], "By your life, In the end you will concede to their words." And [so] he commanded one of his students to test her with a matter of sin. And [that student] pleaded with her many days until she agreed. And when she found out, she strangled herself. And [so] Rabbi Meir ran away due to embarrassment.
Mishnah: "We do not place an animal in gentile inns" - This refers to inns where travelers lodge and pay the owners for accommodations.

"Because they are suspected of bestiality" - The descendants of Noah (gentiles) are prohibited from such acts, as it is written, "They shall become one flesh" (Genesis 2:24), which excludes animals, wild creatures, and birds. Allowing this would violate the prohibition of "Do not place a stumbling block before the blind."

“נשג”א” – The sages decreed impurity regarding them (Gentile women) for the matter of niddah (ritual impurity related to menstruation) on a rabbinic level. And even though a Gentile woman’s blood does not cause impurity according to Torah law, since she is compared to an animal, the sages decreed it. They also decreed impurity for a maidservant (shifchah) due to her status as a Gentile woman, as if one were to enter into a marital relationship with her. And concerning a married woman (eshet ish), Gentiles do have the concept of being considered a “married woman” (be’ulat ba’al), as it is written, “and she is [another man’s] wife” (Genesis 20:3). And regarding an Israelite who is accustomed to engaging with them: since he would be with her while she is in a state of niddah, he may come to have relations with a Jewish woman while she is in niddah. Furthermore, he may come to marry a maidservant, thereby violating the prohibition of “There shall not be a harlot among the daughters of Israel” (Deuteronomy 23:18). He may also come to marry a Gentile woman, violating the prohibition of “You shall not intermarry with them” (Deuteronomy 7:3). And he may come to have relations with a married Jewish woman (eshet ish Yisrael).
And this that he was holding a dry measure and he was measuring, this is prohibited on account of Yosef.  However the face of man in general is permitted for benefit.

Mishnah: If a gentile hires a Jew to perform work with wine used for idolatry—such as to pour it from one vessel to another, or to carry a cask from place to place. And it speaks here specifically about actual Yayin Nesech (wine that has been offered to idol worship). But regarding Stam Yeinam (ordinary gentile wine not known to have been offered), the Gemara raises the question.

If [the non-Jew] hired him to perform another kind of work (not connected with the wine) — then all of his wages are permitted, because even though he is giving him payment, it is not considered as being given on account of the [forbidden] work with the wine, but rather for the other work. And the Gemara explains this matter clearly.

Gemara: [Case of] “Mekudeshet” (betrothal is valid) — this would imply that with things forbidden in benefit (issurei hana’ah), their monetary value is still permitted, and all the more so wages for his labor [should be permitted].

But — since [in the case of Yayin Nesech] its monetary value is seized like that of idolatry — for once it has been libated to idol worship, it becomes like actual idolatry, and its value is prohibited. As it says earlier (Avodah Zarah 54b): “Anything from which one derives [forbidden benefit] is considered like itself.” Therefore, just as its value is forbidden, so too the wages for his labor are forbidden.
Gather for me with it — this is an expression of sale, meaning “gather for me its value in vegetables.”
His wages are forbidden — i.e., to keep them beyond the time of bi’ur (removal) [in the Sabbatical year], but rather they must be disposed of during Shevi’it.
Gather for me vegetables — this is an expression of rental/hire, not of sale, and therefore it does not acquire monetary value that would be seized with the sanctity of Shevi’it.
A case of permission - when it is given as a free gift
As we learned (in a Mishnah) - regarding Ma’aser Sheni
To divide it - that you should take a share from it, because it is forbidden to repay a debt with Ma’aser Sheni — even though, he also eats it in Jerusalem.

And our Mishnah - [discussing]  Yayin Nesech, where the Sages penalized even the labourer (that he cannot keep his wages) [despite] his wages are not large, the stringency of Yayin Nesech is different.
Because its prohibition is severe - since it is forbidden in benefit like actual Yayin Nesech itself.

But in terms of ritual impurity it is lighter - as we said earlier (Avodah Zarah 30a): There are three kinds of wine, Yayin Nesech: forbidden in benefit and conveys severe tum’ah with an olive’s volume. Stam Yeinam: forbidden in benefit but conveys liquid impurity only with a quarter-log.
Ship - his ship.
A cemetery – a cemetery.
He should scatter them as they - He should scatter them as they are; why is there a requirement to burn them.
Will come to – because people may come to a mishap, gathering them back up again.
He should bury them - As they are, in that very state.

All of them are buried with him – as it is written (Devarim 21:23): “His body shall not remain overnight upon the tree, but you shall surely bury him” — this includes even the tree itself. And we also say in (Sanhedrin 46b) chapter Nigmar HaDin: The tree, I might have thought whether it was cut or still attached — therefore Scripture says: “You shall surely bury him” — only something that lacks burial, not something that requires both uprooting and burial. this excludes something that requires both burial and uprooting. Thus, the tree itself is considered assur b’hana’ah and is buried with him as-is, and we are not concerned that someone might come to wrongdoing.

There it is different, since they are buried by the court - In cemeteries designated by the court; it is evident to all who find them there, that they came from those executed by Beit Din, and they will leave them alone.
One lent fruits of the Sabbatical year - Before the time of bi’ur (removal).
And he repaid them in the eighth year - It turns out that the poor are eating in the eighth year after bi'ur,  produce that came in exchange of Shemitah fruits.

This is correct - Since at that time [the Shemitah-fruits] these were no longer extant, and there was no direct exchange; therefore they are not considered a “substitute” (chalifin) and the sanctity of Shemitah does not rest upon them.

And in the corresponding case concerning payment to a prostitute - If one cohabited with a harlot and afterward gave her her fee (etnan), the animal is permitted for sacrifice. That since he did not give it at the time of the intercourse, when he later gave it to her that lamb is considered only an ordinary gift.
If he gave her but did not cohabit yet, etc. — the Gemara goes on to explain this.
Rather this is what it means: he gave her (payment) - And did not cohabit with her immediately, only after a period of time.
Or he cohabited with her - And did not give her payment immediately; only after a period of time.
The prohibition of etnan (harlot’s wage) should take effect retroactively -  Since he gave it to her at the outset on condition of intercourse.

Acquire it from now - Before intercourse, it is obvious that it is permitted, for even though he gave it on condition of intercourse, since he gave it to her before intercourse, it is not considered payment for intercourse.

If you will need it, acquire it from now - Therefore the Mishnah needed to teach us that even though he said to her, “It shall not be acquired to you until the moment of intercourse”, since he then said, “If you will need it, acquire it from now,” it is considered a free gift. [Therefore] when she [later] takes it and offers it [as a sacrifice, it is valid].
Since the Master said - In the Tosefta in Kiddushin, chapter 1 (28b).
With THIS lamb - Whenever he gives it to her, it is considered an etnan, because from now she acquires it.
With an unspecified lamb  – When he gives it after a period of time, it is not considered an etnan, because only now she acquires it.

A gentile does not acquire with meshichah (pulling/physical delivery), for when Scripture wrote about meshichah, it wrote it regarding Israel (Vayikra 25:14) — “or acquired from the hand of your people.
He had already acquired it - From now, before the intercourse, so how can we call it “he cohabited with her and afterward gave it to her”?

If he did not take it - [Saying "If I don't compensate you] prior to a certain date, then it shall be your etnan”. It is therefore considered as if he cohabited and afterward gave it. However, since from the moment of the intercourse he designated it as a specific security (apoteki), and it was already standing in her courtyard, [the prohibition of] etnan takes effect
Rav Sheshet raised an objection - To R. Yannai.
His workers and his donkey-drivers - [Either] gentiles or amei ha’aretz (unlearned Jews).

Not because of Shevi‘it - Lest they take Shevi‘it produce from someone suspected of selling it. And it was taught in Sukkah (39a) One may not hand over the money of Shevi‘it produce to an am ha’aretz more than the value of three meals.

Nor because of ma‘aser (tithes) - For if they are amei ha’aretz and buy produce that is not tithed, it would turn out that this man causes them to eat untithed produce. But here he is not actually feeding them anything directly — he only gives them coins.

Nor because of yayin nesech (forbidden wine) - If they are gentiles, it would turn out he is causing them to drink yayin nesech, since he is responsible for their food, and thus he benefits from yayin nesech.
And I will pay - He himself is (effectively) the one purchasing the prohibition and feeding them. For now he has not withdrawn himself from it with the coins.
Who extends him credit - Who regularly extends him credit.
There is a lien on him - That employer: from the moment the shopkeeper gives produce [to the worker], it is as if he gave it directly into the workers’ hands.

[The shopkeeper] acquires the dinar that is with him [the employer] - The shopkeeper relies on this, as he is familiar with him [the employer]. that wherever the dinar is located, it is acquired by the shopkeeper, therefore it is a proper exchange. But those in the case of the household of R. Yannai, since the poor who lend them the produce are not shopkeepers who regularly extend them credit, they do not rely to the same extent [as the shopkeepers in getting repaid], and there is no real lien on the household of R. Yannai. Therefore when they repay at a later time [after prohibition] it is not considered an exchange of Shevi'it produce
If so - That the reason [it is forbidden] is the shopkeeper regularly gives him credit, but if he does not normally give credit it is permissible.

Why learn - In the first case, where the Tanna is looking for a case which is permitted, and only found the scenario of go out and eat with this dinar [that he hands to them] and thus removes himself with [handing over] these coins.

Let there be a [narrower] differentiation and learn - The permitted scenario, even when he has not removed himself [entirely], for example in the case of go and out and I will pay, and where the shopkeeper does not normally extend him credit and therefore there is no lien on the employer. And all the more so [it will be permitted] where he removes himself entirely
Further a shopkeeper who is not his credit-giver – If he gave [produce] to the householder’s messenger.

Does he not become obligated - to him [the shopkeeper]; the householder from that moment [of handing over the produce]. [And how is it] that you permitted the house of Rabbi Yannai based on this reasoning?
And Rava said: One who says to his fellow, “Give a maneh to so-and-so, and my property shall be acquired to you - With that maneh and he gave it.
He acquires it - The purchaser, the [donors] property, even though the benefit of that maneh did not reach him.

By the law of a guarantor - From that dinar {alternative text 'from that law'} that a guarantor becomes obligated to pay even though no benefit reached him. And here too it is the same. It follows, then, that even when it is not his regular shopkeeper, if he gave to his [the employer’s] messenger, the householder becomes obligated [from now].

Rather, Rava said - Do not teach that the reason of the baraita was “because of the lien” (shi’abuda), and only when it is his regular shopkeeper. For even when it is not his regular shopkeeper, a lien exists. However as for the house of R. Yannai there is no difficulty, as whether it was a regular shopkeeper or not.
Even though there is a lien - Assets to pay.
Since he did not designate a lien - He did not immediately designate money to him for this, it is not a proper exchange, and therefore the prohibition [of Shevi‘it does not transfer].
This is the correct version: 'And here Rav Pappa said' and we do not read 'Rather here the baraita says we are concerned says Rav Pappa'
When he advanced him - The employer a dinar to the shopkeeper before sending them [the workers] to him, that now they are eating directly from the employer’s money, and the prohibition is upon him.
And I will pay - He has already paid.
It should say and I will calculate - I will make a calculation from that which I have already given him.

That he handled - From the hands of the shopkeeper and gave to them, that now he is [directly] supplying them with the prohibited, and this is not because of the later payment, rather he acquires it with Meshicha (handling of the goods), and it transpires that he has taken possession of wine used for libation and given it to drink to his workers. But the house of R. Yannai when they take possession of the produce it is at a permitted time, and when they subsequently compensate at the time Shevi'it is forbidden it is no longer considered an exchange that effects a transfer [of the  restrictions]
Go - Implies that he is not going with them (to the shop).
To break the yayin nesech - To break barrels, and to pour out the wine.
What is the law - That the wages are permitted?
Do we say since - That this Jew wants these barrels to remain intact, that the should not break by themselves, until he breaks them and takes payment it should be forbidden?
One may not hoe - May not dig
Leavidrona - Name of a non-jew.
In roses - In a bathhouse of roses.
May any eye that wishes to see evil upon you - The eye that desires to see  your harm should be uprooted, for behold HKB"H fulfils all your desires even your [mundane] talk is clarified.
Your honour - In order to honour you. The prophet is informing the Jewish [nation].
No eye has seen it - Apart from the eye of HKB'H, that which will be done to those who waits for Him, never has there been seen glory and greatness like it.

And even though - That the transferring of a cask is not at the time of evening, after the whole period of his hire has been completed, but rather before the conclusion of the time of his hire, he said to him: “Transfer a cask of wine used for idolatry”, the Mishnah teaches that his wage is permitted? [this is stated] with astonishment.
At evening time – For his entire wage had already been obligated to him before the transferring of the cask.
Rava said - Actually he did not say to him towards evening.

And there is no difficulty - Our Mishne that teaches it is permissible, is a case of transport for me each barrel for a Prutah,  and when it transpires there is a barrel of Yayin Nesech amongst them, throw a Prutah into the river or alternatively do not take it from the non-jew and the balance will be permitted, because the payment for that barrel is not connected with the others as each (barrel) is rewarded independently: And the Braissoh  is [discussing] when he did not say to him towards evening, where all the wages are forbidden, is a case where he says transport form me 100 barrels for 100 Prutahs, that as long as he has not transported all of them he will not be given any (payment) at all, therefore the whole payment is connected to it [the barrel of Yayin Nesech]

Mishne: If it was in a status of being supervised - In the Gemoroh it explains that even though the Jew had distanced himself from the gentile a mil(e) if he did not inform him he was separating the (wine) is permitted  for the gentile is constantly afraid all the time now [at any moment] he is coming [back].
If he let him know that he is separating - That he is distancing himself and the barrels were sealed.

The amount [of time allowed] that it would take the gentile to pierce and reseal, and for the seal to dry out - If he tarried the amount of time that the gentile could pierce a hole in the seal of the barrel, and subsequently reseal the hole, so that the seal would be dry [the wine] is forbidden.

RSB'G states - It is not forbidden until the delay is as long as it would take him to open the complete seal of the barrel [i.e. remove the lid], and it would be impossible to remove it without breaking it completely.
And seal - And make another new seal/lid.

And dry - And it would dry, but as for piercing a hole they are not concerned as it would be noticeable. The word Shesum is defined (in the expression) Shesum Ho-ayin (Numbers 34:3 describing Billam) an open eye that has good vision.
One who places his wine in a wagon or boat - Together with a gentile.
And went - The Jew via a shortcut, a shorter route.
And entered the district and bathed - In a bathhouse, it [the wine] is permitted, since the gentile did not know of the delay, he is afraid and will not touch it.
Side table - The old French word (as translated by Kugovitzki in Sefer Tirgemi Laaz is) cupboard. [This side table or cupboard was using for preparing and storing food prior to bringing to the table]
What is on the table is forbidden - This gentile will tell himself that this Jew invited me to eat and drink and [will therefore] touch [the wine].
On the side table [the wine] is permitted - For it has not been prepared for this meal.

If [the Jew] told him dilute [the wine] and drink - Since he has reinforced his hand by giving [albeit] some minimal permission, [the gentile] will feel confident and touch everything [including the side table].
Open barrels - That are in the house are forbidden.

Sealed [barrels] are permitted - Until he delays [the amount of time] that it would take to [break] open [the lid], reseal and for the seal to dry and this defaults to the opinion of R. Shimon, as it does not teach [just] piercing [the seal of the barrel].

What is different regarding the first clause and what is different with the latter clause - He [the owner] sees that they are [directly] touching [the pure produce] as it teaches they [the ignorant workers] were loading the pure produce and this case is not discussing barrels that would have been sealed.
Where he purified is donkey drivers - He made them [have a ritual] dip, and therefore their touching [pure items] leaves them pure.
On the touching by his acquaintance  - The one he bumps into on the route, and [this acquaintance]  has not been purified for this [purpose of touching pure items].
In the first case also - since he has distanced himself, one should [also] be concerned for this [same possibility of meeting an impure acquaintance].
In that he came in a roundabout way - When the owner is able to come in a roundabout way [twisted pathway] he [the worker] will be afraid that now [any moment] he may come.
Had it taught [just the case of] a gentile - A gentile who is transporting flagons of wine.
And do whatever he wants - Even if he did not inform him that he is distancing himself it would be forbidden.

The argument is with lime - With a seal of lime, which is white, in that case the Rabbis are concerned that [the gentile] will pierce [the seal of the barrel], since it [the lime] is white one cannot differentiate between new and old [seals]. {R. Shimon argues that one could tell from the inside of the lid that the filled in hole would not be to exactly the same depth as the rest}

But with cement - That is initially dark and even when it dries out, it still doesn't turn white for a day or two, everybody agrees we are not concerned for piercing [alone of the seal] because the resealing of the pierced hole would be distinguished against the rest of the seal, it would only be forbidden [if the amount of time taken would be] to open, and reseal a new lid and dry out
and is not his sealing recognisable - If he pierces a hole, behold it is apparent.
Whether above - That this is new, and the sealed lid is old.

Whether below - When a Jew opens the sealed lid he will see the bottom of that [new] seal[ed hole], that above has been smoothed by the gentile and the seal levelled, but below [at the bottom of the hole] he is unable to rub [and smooth] it, and it will be noticed.
Rather if you say it is lime - that the Rabbis [are disputing], it is not recognisable that he resealed the top, so how could it teach [it is noticeable] whether above or below.

It is sound - The hole gets filled at the bottom just like at the top {i.e. filled all the way through and neatly levelled off at both ends} . Cholim (Dayan I Gukovitzki: Tirgemei Halaz) Solder\Weld in old French.
Is it not obvious - The author of the Mishne closed in accordance with him [R. Shimon's opinion]. Is Rava coming to tell us something that is [documented] in a Mishne?

I might have thought - That the case [at the end of the Mishne] that he was eating together with him at the table is the conclusion of the statement of R. Shimon, and he [R. Shimon] is the one teaching it. And this is how to understand the Mishne: R. Shimon states in order that he can open reseal and dry out, {continuing R Shimon's opinion with} he was eating with him etc.. And this is not an independent closing statement by the author of the Mishne {which would determine the Halacha}. Therefore Rava teaches us it is an independent concluding statement.

And now we have established the Halacha like R. Shimon that we are not concerned for sealing  - a pierced hole which can be done without effort, because it can be discerned, and additionally entirely opening the lid, that R. Shimon is concerned for, we do not establish [the halacha] like him, because that type of forging involves effort, and we have established in (Chapter) Eiyn Mamidim (earlier daf 31a) the halacha is in accordance with R. Eliezer whom is not concerned for the forgery of [even] a single seal. For why did we not question him from [our case here of] sealed barrels in the hand of gentiles {where there is concern even according to R Shimon of possible forgery}.

Because of the slot - Extremely narrow hole in the bung of the barrel, to enable the wine vapours to escape. There is a concern that perhaps it may have been somewhat bored and he [the gentile] will have tasted of the wine.
The pressing desire for Yayin Nesech is not strong for them - For them to make a libation.
She is dragged [forced] after them - That she allows them to make the libation.
In line with that crack is permitted - Even to drink, for he is afraid and would not touch.

That on this side and on that side is forbidden - Even to derive just benefit {as opposed to drinking}. The situation we are dealing with is when he is not seized on entry like as a thief. That he owned a portion of the wine, for if he were to be seized as a thief all of it would be permitted. - There are those whose text read Bizyeini {rather than Bizoh} Bedasha [which implies] a number of holes cracks and fissures. The word {in scriptures} Uvkohayhu is translated by the Targum as Uvezohu [fissures].
The Jew in the upper story and the gentile in the lower story - The wine was in the lower story and it was visible to the Jew upstairs.

It is permitted - All {cases} here where it states permitted, is defined as permitted to drink, for we are dealing with situations where no touching took place, and wherever here it states forbidden it is forbidden to even derive any benefit. And in all these cases the Halacha is like Rava.

If he can push matters off [with a justifiable excuse] - And say for this purpose I entered, he will feel secure and will not be afraid {to touch the wine}, for when he entered the house he entered with the  intention of libation, and thinks [to himself] if they find me I can push them off. Even though with regard to touching the wine he has no justifiable reason, [nevertheless the wine] is forbidden, for if he did not intend to make a libation why did he enter? We cannot compare this to the {earlier} case of leaving a gentile in one's shop {and the wine is not forbidden}, because there the gentile entered with permission {presumably to buy wine} and we know why he entered  [the shop], so as long as the owner does not inform him he is leaving [the wine is permitted] as he [the gentile] thinks to himself if I touch the wine now [the owner] will come in and see. {Rashi  makes a very suttle difference between the two cases. In both cases the gentile is allowed to be there. The suttle difference is in the case of the shop we know exactly why he is in the shop, in the case of our Gemoroh, although he can give a valid reason why he entered, but we do not know for what purpose he entered and the default assumption is, his intention is to make wine libations}.
And if - he cannot push off [has no justifiable reason why he is there], and since he is anxious [for even] entering, he is afraid and will not [go on to] touch.
The innkeeper locked the door - And the gentile was secluded with the wine, or the Jew said to the gentile guard [meaning] stand outside and guard.

It is forbidden - We are concerned that perhaps he went up [in], since he [the Jew] told him [the gentile] 'guard' he [the gentile] feels secure that he [the Jew] has separated [distanced] himself from him.
The Shofar of twilight - Of Erev Shabos that they would blow to distinguish between holy {Sabbath} and mundane {weekdays}.
And if because of the Sabbath - And if you are going to suggest that the gentile will rely [on the fact] that the Jew will not come [return] on the Sabbath, I was told by Issur the Convert etc.
Less less than 4 cubits - And one stops to rest [within 4 cubits], so that there is no uplift from the start of the 4 cubits to the end of [full] 4 cubits. {and thus  avoids transgressing}.
Hide - Hide himself.
Mishnah. A vat [for wine-pressing] made of stone that a heathen [sealed with] tar: it was customary to lift a small amount of wine into it [i.e. the vat] to overcome the smell of the tar.
To scour it: [This is] explained in the gemara [as scouring using] water and ashes.
Of wood: which requires more tar since it absorbs more wine [i.e. than a stone vat]. Rabbi says scour it as with the stone [vat] and the Sages disagree.
And of earthenware, even if the tar is peeled off, it is forbidden: one might think every opinion holds this way since earthenware itself without tar absorbs wine.
Gemara. But if he trampled [grapes] in it [i.e. the vat]: without tarring, scouring is not necessary, rather rinsing [is sufficient].
He taught the customary case: because it is the custom of the tar-sealers to throw wine into it [i.e. the vat].
Others say, Raba says only when tarred: [if the vat is tarred, but] he did not trample [grapes] in it, this is the case in which scouring is sufficient.
Cleansing it is not sufficient - rather, peeling [off the pitch entirely is necessary] because wine may enter the cracks in the pitch.
Shi'ah - Smooth.

And they do not disagree. Rav and Shmuel [do not disagree], according to the language of Pumbedita, except that Rav does not count the final [rinsing with] water, and Shmuel does count the final [rinsing with] water. And there are those who explain that "they do not disagree" refers to Sura and Pumbedita, except that Sura does not count the final [rinsing with] water and that Pumbedita does count [the final rinsing]; but, Rav and Shmuel disagree. And this is the meaning of the words "two, three": Two [steps are necessary] for a dry [vat]: water and ash; three for a moist [vat]: ash and water and ash. And Shmuel says three for a moist [vat] as stated, but for a dry [vat], four: water and ash, water and ash; in all cases, [Shmuel] requires ash twice. And in Pumbedita it was taught that Rav [required] three and four [steps]: For a dry [vat], three: water and ash [and] water. And we also have this in Sura, except these [i.e. the Pumbedita prescriptions] count final water [for rinsing]. And for a moist [vat], four [steps are required]: ash and water, ash and water; and according to Shmuel, for a moist [vat], four [steps are required] as stated, but for a dry [vat] five [steps are required]: water and ash, and water and ash, and water, such that a dry [vat] also requires ash twice. "And they do not disagree refers to Sura and Pumbedita, etc." But, Rav and Shmuel disagree regarding a dry [vat] both in Sura and in Pumbedita in that Rav only requires ash once and Shmuel requires [ash] twice. This is reading of my father, my teacher, may he rest in peace, and this seems to me [to be the correct reading]. The first reading [is that of] my teacher, and it is difficult for me since in the language of Sura, Rav and Shmuel certainly disagree. What is the difference [of opinion]? Rav counts final [rinsing] water and Shmuel does not count final [rinsing] water. For Shmuel, [the] four and five [counting] requires that we teach [that Shmuel is counting the final rinsing water]. This is reasonable according to Pumbedita even though Rav does not count [the final rinsing water] and Shmuel does count [it]. This is convenient because the disagreement between Rav and Shmuel is not substantive, [it is] only [a disparity] in the counting of the final [rinsing] water. But, according to the language of Sura, there is still a disagreement [between Rav and Shmuel], which is difficult for me.

Gurgei - [wicker-net] bales, in La'az "ributi," [which] are wrapped around the "tapuach" [i.e. heap of grape pulp] so that the grapes do not scatter because of the weight of the beam [which is used to press them]. And Rav Hai [Gaon] commented [that] "akalim" as taught here are like "a bale ["ekel"] [used for] an olive press" (Sanhedrin 26a), made as a type of basket weaved into a net. After squeezing the olives the "gefet" [i.e. peat made of olive peals] is placed in that "ekel" [i.e. wicker-net] and [one] presses it [with a beam] and because of the weight [being applied] the remaining drink is drawn [from the peat made of olive peals]. These are "gurgei d'Armaei" [i.e. the wicker-nets of the Gentiles]. How is it scoured?
This is the vat itself, which is called "Mait" [Old French: the bin portion of a wine-press].
Hemp, which is very absorptive, and requires scouring with ash and water.
"Paveil" [Old French: a type of rush].
"Jonc" [Old French: rush], which is very absorptive.
A pot in which an idolater [non-Jew] cooked today, but if he cooked in it yesterday, its taste has already deteriorated overnight, and when it later emits flavor it is only for spoilage.
'King Shapur' -- He was a gentile.
'דצה' -- He stabbed it.
'I am certain regarding this master' -- 'I know that Rav Yehudah is meticulous and will not eat a forbidden food, but I am not certain about you that you would be so meticulous.'

'What you did at night' -- It was the way of the Persians to give women to their guests, and when they sent [the women] to them the previous night, Bati received [the woman], but Rav Yehudah did not recieve [the woman].
